summary.text: Fermat's Last Theorem says there are no positive integers a, b, c, n with n > 2 such that aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ.
Around 1637 Fermat wrote in a book's margin that he had a marvelous proof, but he left no details and none has ever been found.
Andrew Wiles released the first successful proof in 1994, after 358 years of effort, and it was formally published in 1995.

facts.label: Years of effort
facts.value: 358 years before the first successful proof

facts.label: Easy cases
facts.value: n = 1 and n = 2 have infinitely many solutions

facts.label: Wiles's honour
facts.value: Abel Prize 2016, citing a stunning advance

items.prompt: A teacher shows that 3, 4 and 5 satisfy x² + y² = z². A student asks if that breaks the theorem. What is the answer?

options.label: Yes, because 3, 4 and 5 are all positive whole numbers
No, the theorem only rules out powers above 2
Yes, but only because 5 is not a perfect square
No, because the theorem bans every power except 1

items.explain: The squares equation has infinitely many positive integer solutions, such as 3, 4, 5. The theorem concerns exponents greater than 2.

items.prompt: Fermat claimed a marvelous proof, yet nobody could find it or build one for centuries. What label did the claim end up with?

options.label: A proven theorem, because Fermat said so
A conjecture, because no proof was ever found
A disproved claim, because a counterexample appeared
A definition, because it was stated in a margin

items.explain: Because Fermat's proof never surfaced and the statement resisted proof, it became known as a conjecture rather than a theorem.

items.prompt: Mathematicians checking the claim looked mostly at prime exponents. Why could they skip the others?

options.label: Non-prime exponents are known to be impossible to test
Fermat proved the claim for every non-prime exponent directly
Non-prime exponents give the same answer as the exponent 2
A failure at a non-prime exponent would force a failure at a smaller one

items.explain: The case of exponent 4, proved by Fermat, shows that if the theorem is false for a non-prime exponent, it is false for some smaller one, so only primes need study.

items.prompt: Two apparently unrelated problems were linked in the 1980s. What did the link say about a counterexample to Fermat's claim?

options.label: It could also be used to contradict the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture
It would make the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture automatically true
It would have no bearing on elliptic curves
It would show the Pythagorean equation has no solutions

items.explain: Any solution that could contradict Fermat's Last Theorem could also be used to contradict the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture, so proving that conjecture settles Fermat's claim.

items.prompt: Computers verified the claim for every prime exponent up to four million. Does that settle the theorem?

options.label: Yes, since four million exponents is more than anyone could need
Yes, because primes are the only exponents that matter
No, a proof must cover all exponents, which was seen as exceedingly difficult
No, because computers cannot handle exponents at all

items.explain: The theorem covers every exponent above 2, so checking up to four million is not a proof; a proof for all exponents was considered exceedingly difficult at that time.

items.prompt: Some people picture Wiles rediscovering the proof Fermat hinted at. What does the record say about the mathematics used?

options.label: It used only methods that Fermat himself used
It was solved with mathematics Fermat would not have known
It was a short argument fitting in a margin
It relied only on the Pythagorean triples

items.explain: The claim stayed unsolved for three and a half centuries and was solved with mathematics that Fermat would not have known.
